section.heading: 5.4 Comparison Tests
Learning Objectives

list.item: Use the comparison test to test a series for convergence.
Use the limit comparison test to determine convergence of a series.

section.paragraph: We have seen that the integral test allows us to determine the convergence or divergence of a series by comparing it to a related improper integral. In this section, we show how to use comparison tests to determine the convergence or divergence of a series by comparing it to a series whose convergence or divergence is known. Typically these tests are used to determine convergence of series that are similar to geometric series or p-series.
section.heading: Comparison Test
section.paragraph: In the preceding two sections, we discussed two large classes of series: geometric series and p-series. We know exactly when these series converge and when they diverge. Here we show how to use the convergence or divergence of these series to prove convergence or divergence for other series, using a method called the comparison test.

Suppose there exists an integer $$N$$ such that $$a_{n} \geq b_{n} \geq 0$$ for all $$n \geq N.$$ If $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}b_{n}$$ diverges, then $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ diverges.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: We prove part i. The proof of part ii. is the contrapositive of part i. Let $$\left\{ S_{k} \right\}$$ be the sequence of partial sums associated with $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n},$$ and let $$L = \sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}b_{n}.$$ Since the terms $$a_{n} \geq 0,$$
Therefore, the sequence of partial sums is increasing. Further, since $$a_{n} \leq b_{n}$$ for all $$n \geq N,$$ then
$$S_{k} = \left( {a_{1} + a_{2} + \text{⋯} + a_{N - 1}} \right) + {\sum\limits_{n = N}^{k}{a_{n} \leq}}\left( {a_{1} + a_{2} + \text{⋯} + a_{N - 1}} \right) + L.$$

Since $$a_{1} + a_{2} + \text{⋯} + a_{N - 1}$$ is a finite number, we conclude that the sequence $$\left\{ S_{k} \right\}$$ is bounded above. Therefore, $$\left\{ S_{k} \right\}$$ is an increasing sequence that is bounded above. By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, we conclude that $$\left\{ S_{k} \right\}$$ converges, and therefore the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ converges.

To use the comparison test to determine the convergence or divergence of a series $${\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}},$$ it is necessary to find a suitable series with which to compare it. Since we know the convergence properties of geometric series and p-series, these series are often used. If there exists an integer $$N$$ such that for all $$n \geq N,$$ each term $$a_{n}$$ is less than each corresponding term of a known convergent series, then $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ converges. Similarly, if there exists an integer $$N$$ such that for all $$n \geq N,$$ each term $$a_{n}$$ is greater than each corresponding term of a known divergent series, then $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}$$ diverges.

problem.paragraph: For each of the following series, use the comparison test to determine whether the series converges or diverges.

list.item: Compare to $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{3}}$$ Since $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{3}}$$ is a p-series with $$p = 3,$$ it converges. Further, $$\frac{1}{n^{3} + 3n + 1} < \frac{1}{n^{3}}$$ for every positive integer $$n.$$ Therefore, we can conclude that $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{3} + 3n + 1}$$ converges.

Compare to $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n}.$$ Since $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n}$$ is a geometric series with $$r = 1/2$$ and $$\left| 1/2 \middle| < 1, \right.$$ it converges. Also, $$\frac{1}{2^{n} + 1} < \frac{1}{2^{n}}$$ for every positive integer $$n.$$ Therefore, we see that $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n} + 1}$$ converges.

Compare to $$\sum\limits_{n = 2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}.$$ Since $$\frac{1}{\ln (n)} > \frac{1}{n}$$ for every integer $$n \geq 2$$ and $$\sum\limits_{n = 2}^{\infty}1/n$$ diverges, we have that $$\sum\limits_{n = 2}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\ln (n)}$$ diverges.

section.paragraph: Note that if $$a_{n}/b_{n}\rightarrow 0$$ and $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}b_{n}$$ diverges, the limit comparison test gives no information. Similarly, if $$a_{n}/b_{n}\rightarrow\infty$$ and $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}b_{n}$$ converges, the test also provides no information. For example, consider the two series $${\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}1}/\sqrt{n}$$ and $${\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}1}/n^{2}.$$ These series are both p-series with $$p = 1/2$$ and $$p = 2,$$ respectively. Since $$p = 1/2 < 1,$$ the series $${\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}1}/\sqrt{n}$$ diverges. On the other hand, since $$p = 2 > 1,$$ the series $${\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}1}/n^{2}$$ converges. However, suppose we attempted to apply the limit comparison test, using the convergent $$p - \text{series}$$ $${\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}1}/n^{3}$$ as our comparison series. First, we see that

Therefore, if $$a_{n}/b_{n}\rightarrow\infty$$ when $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}b_{n}$$ converges, we do not gain any information on the convergence or divergence of $${\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}a_{n}}.$$

problem.paragraph: For each of the following series, use the limit comparison test to determine whether the series converges or diverges. If the test does not apply, say so.

list.item: Compare this series to $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}.$$ Calculate $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim } \frac{1/(\sqrt{n} + 1)}{1/\sqrt{n}} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\begin{matrix} \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{n} + 1} \\ \end{matrix} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim } \frac{1}{1 + 1/\sqrt{n}} = 1.$$ By the limit comparison test, since $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$$ diverges, then $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n} + 1}$$ diverges.

Compare this series to $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)^{n}.$$ We see that $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{(2^{n} + 1)/3^{n}}{2^{n}/3^{n}} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{2^{n} + 1}{3^{n}} \cdot \frac{3^{n}}{2^{n}} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{2^{n} + 1}{2^{n}} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\left\lbrack {1 + \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n}} \right\rbrack = 1.$$ Therefore, $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{(2^{n} + 1)/3^{n}}{2^{n}/3^{n}} = 1.$$ Since $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)^{n}$$ converges, we conclude that $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{2^{n} + 1}{3^{n}}$$ converges.

Since $$\ln n < n,$$ compare with $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}.$$ We see that $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln n/n^{2}}{1/n} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln n}{n^{2}} \cdot \frac{n}{1} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln n}{n}.$$ In order to evaluate $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\ln n/n,$$ evaluate the limit as $$x\rightarrow\infty$$ of the real-valued function $$\ln (x)/x.$$ These two limits are equal, and making this change allows us to use L’Hôpital’s rule. We obtain $$\underset{x\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln x}{x} = \underset{x\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{1}{x} = 0.$$ Therefore, $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\ln n/n = 0,$$ and, consequently, $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln n/n^{2}}{1/n} = 0.$$ Since the limit is $$0$$ but $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}$$ diverges, the limit comparison test does not provide any information. Compare with $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}$$ instead. In this case, $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln n/n^{2}}{1/n^{2}} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln n}{n^{2}} \cdot \frac{n^{2}}{1} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\ln n = \infty.$$ Since the limit is $$\infty$$ but $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}$$ converges, the test still does not provide any information. So now we try a series between the two we already tried. Choosing the series $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{3/2}},$$ we see that $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln n/n^{2}}{1/n^{3/2}} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln n}{n^{2}} \cdot \frac{n^{3/2}}{1} = \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln n}{\sqrt{n}}.$$ As above, in order to evaluate $$\underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\ln n/\sqrt{n},$$ evaluate the limit as $$x\rightarrow\infty$$ of the real-valued function $$\ln x/\sqrt{x}.$$ Using L’Hôpital’s rule, $$\underset{x\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{x}} = \underset{x\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{x} = \underset{x\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\frac{2}{\sqrt{x}} = 0.$$ Since the limit is $$0$$ and $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{3/2}}$$ converges, we can conclude that $$\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}\frac{\ln n}{n^{2}}$$ converges.
